name: Iris Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. This conversation is confidential. What is an ordinary day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Iris Usman, 43, a junior construction worker fitting access ramps and rails on public building sites. I left school early and still ask the lead carpenter to check where my first bracket goes. The public hall contract pays better than most of my earlier work. I sometimes use an AI app to explain a plan term, but I want to see a method work on a real wall before I trust it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the family need from your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works at a dental reception desk, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. We have saved about ten months of expenses. My pay helps us stay ahead of the loan, and my partner’s clinic hours make the school run possible when I start early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a bit of office automation may tidy the ramp materials order, but we still need to fit the rails to the old hall wall. I sometimes ask an AI app what a term on a plan means, then ask the site carpenter. I would not call a faster form a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 43 and still learning general carpentry, with the lead carpenter checking my rail brackets. The public hall contract pays above the usual rate, my partner works at a dental reception desk, and we have ten months of bills saved. The mortgage is real, but the small AI change does not make me expect either wage to disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working on the hall ramps and ask for a check before drilling each first bracket. In the first year I'd continue putting the contract premium into our mortgage account when it arrives. If an unfamiliar plan term comes up, I'd use the AI app once, then confirm it with the carpenter before acting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like a bit less paperwork at the site office. I still care more about whether someone using a walking frame can grip the rail than whether a form arrives in seconds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the wall teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The plaster looked flat until we pulled a loose patch away and found old brick behind it. The carpenter changed the fixing method before I drilled. A printed plan could not see that wall any better than an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your partner use AI at the desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner uses the clinic’s booking system, but I do not know whether it has AI inside it. We talk about the day’s patients only in broad terms. For now the reception hours are steady, and our children still have school routines to manage.

say: I would say **ordering forms** may speed up while workers still fit hall rails.
I would say a wall needs a **physical check** before drilling.
think: I am a **junior worker** relying on a carpenter’s bracket checks.
Our **ten-month reserve** and two current wages keep the mortgage secure.
do: Keep paid **hall ramp work** and request first-bracket checks.
Put contract **premium pay** into the mortgage account when received.
Use **AI occasionally** for unfamiliar plan terms, then confirm with the carpenter.
feel: **Calm** about money and focused on whether users can grip the finished rail.
S0.quote: A printed plan could not see that wall any better than an app.
fieldNote: Iris ties her caution to **old brick** behind plaster and the need to change a real fixing method.
The strong **ten-month cushion** and steady reception hours support calm in the mild scenario.

steps.text: Keep paid hall ramp shifts and request first-bracket checks
Put public contract premiums into the mortgage account when received
Use AI for occasional plan terms and confirm meanings with the carpenter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that AI could write orders and book deliveries, while our hands still fit the rails. At home, my partner's reception desk also books appointments and answers patients, so I would not talk as if only other families are affected. I would ask the clinic and the builder for clear notice of changed hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall work may continue, but my partner's desk hours could shrink much sooner than mine. My higher contract pay and savings would cover a gap, though the mortgage was planned around two wages. I do not know whether another clinic would be hiring receptionists if all of them use the same booking tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the hall contractor how orders and shift rosters will change, and my partner would ask the clinic manager about reception hours. I'd use the AI app to understand any new materials list, then check it against the rails on site. In the first year we would set aside the contract premium instead of booking our usual summer trip until we see three months of both payslips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, mainly about two jobs moving at different speeds. I can keep making rails while an office system changes the pay coming through our front door. Our savings help, but they do not answer what work my partner can get next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the summer trip money do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would stay in the account for bills if either set of hours falls. We would still take the children to nearby parks. I would not count money we already have as new saving just because we cancel a booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner after the clinic meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the actual roster and any retraining the clinic offers, then sit with the household budget. My partner is good with people, but I will not assume that protects a desk job from strong thinking AI. We would decide from the hours, not from rumours.

say: I would say **site orders** and my partner’s reception work may both change.
I would ask employers for clear **hour notices** before shifts are cut.
think: My partner’s **reception hours** could shrink before my physical site work.
Ten months saved protects the **mortgage** briefly, but similar desk openings may also shrink.
do: Ask the hall contractor about **rosters** and have my partner ask the clinic about hours.
Use **AI** to understand new material lists, checking them against rails.
Postpone the **summer trip** until three months of both payslips are known.
feel: **Anxious** about two jobs changing at different speeds.
S1.quote: I can keep making rails while an office system changes the pay coming through our front door.
fieldNote: Iris names **household exposure** through dental reception, even while her own rail fitting remains hands-on.
She postpones a **summer trip** but correctly treats the retained cash as existing money, not fresh savings.

steps.text: Keep paid hall ramp shifts while asking the contractor about rosters
Use AI to read new material lists and verify them against site rails
Postpone the family summer trip pending three months of payslips

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 could reach my partner's reception work first, while robots able to fit rails arrive around 2031. It would be foolish to tell the family we have three extra safe years when one wage is at a desk. I would ask both employers for dates, not comforting words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 in 2028 and 48 at the robot date. Our ten-month cushion could handle one lost wage for a while, but not two careers ending. Other building sites are nearby now; if robots spread across them, the number of sites will not tell me how many people they hire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my contract shifts and ask the carpenter to let me practice the more difficult rail returns under supervision. My partner would apply for any paid clinic role involving direct patient help if reception hours fall, though we know that work may change too. In the first year after 2028 I would apply to two building repair crews while still employed, and we would stop spending on the planned second car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, but I can make a list of calls. I would be more worried about my partner's 2028 pay than my own 2031 date at first. If both wages fell, the mortgage would move from a plan to a clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a second car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We had talked about one to ease the school run when my shifts start early. Our current car works, and the children can still get to school without a new one. Buying another loan during a wage change would make me uneasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is direct patient help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner could ask about guiding people through appointments or helping at the clinic desk in person. I cannot promise a clinic would pay for that once AI handles the bookings. Applying would tell us more than guessing at home.

say: I would tell coworkers **reception work** faces 2028 AI before site robots arrive around 2031.
I would ask both employers for **dates and staffing plans**.
think: I would be **48** when capable robots reach my hands-on rail work.
Our cushion cannot carry **two lost careers** through a long mortgage.
do: Keep paid **hall shifts** and practice difficult rail returns.
Apply to **two building repair crews** after 2028 while employed.
Stop the planned **second car** purchase if wages become uncertain.
feel: **Frightened** about the earlier desk risk and later site risk, with calls to make.
S2.quote: Our ten-month cushion could handle one lost wage for a while, but not two careers ending.
fieldNote: Iris correctly sees **two-stage household exposure**: reception by 2028 and physical construction around 2031.
Her own repair applications and partner’s possible **clinic applications** are searches for paid work, with no claim of permanent safety.

steps.text: Keep paid hall shifts and practice rail returns under supervision
Apply to two paid building repair crews after 2028 while employed
Cancel the planned second car purchase during household wage uncertainty

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office and reception desks face the 2031 thinking change, while capable site robots follow around 2034. Five years lets our household watch both employers and reduce debt before either date. I would still ask the builder to show workers what a rail-fitting machine does on an old wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when thinking AI arrives and 51 when robots can do my site work. Our children will be older but may still need us, and I cannot assume the mortgage has disappeared. The extra time helps because my partner can ask about other clinic duties while still earning a reception wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd keep building ramps and ask the carpenter for more practice with uneven walls. My partner would speak to the clinic manager about paid training for patient-facing duties; if a funded place with actual shifts appears, my partner would take it. In the first year after 2031 I'd check building repair openings each month and pay any contract bonus against the mortgage before 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than frightened. There is time to do ordinary careful things, which suits me. I would still feel a jolt if the clinic first cut my partner's hours and the site then tested robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as useful training at the clinic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real shift helping patients, with someone checking the work, and pay during the learning period. A title on a certificate would not cover our mortgage. My partner would ask how many such shifts the clinic expects to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn a robot tool yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the contractor showed that it works safely on an old wall and paid for instruction, I would try it. I already use a phone app occasionally once someone shows the value. I would not pay for a course based on an equipment brochure.

say: I would tell coworkers **2031 desk changes** come before 2034 site robots.
I would ask for a rail-machine trial on an **old wall**.
think: I would be **51** at the robot date, with older children and a possible mortgage.
My partner can explore **paid clinic duties** before reception hours change.
do: Keep paid **ramp shifts** and practice on uneven walls.
Have my partner seek **paid clinic training** with real shifts.
Check **repair openings** monthly after 2031 and pay bonuses toward the mortgage.
feel: **Uneasy** about the two job dates, with time for measured action.
S3.quote: A title on a certificate would not cover our mortgage.
fieldNote: Her partner’s **paid patient-duty training** is conditional on real clinic shifts, not assumed protection from AGI.
Iris is open to **proven site tools** but wants old-wall evidence and paid instruction before adopting one.

steps.text: Keep paid ramp shifts and practice fixing rails on uneven walls
Check paid building repair openings monthly after 2031
Pay contract bonuses toward the mortgage before 2034

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI comes by 2036 and capable robots reach site work around 2039. A decade gives families time to make a proper budget and employers time to show what their machines can do. I would keep learning the trade while paid work is here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the desk change and 56 at the site-robot date. Our children will be grown, so the school run and fees will change, and the mortgage could be much smaller if we keep earning. My partner's reception role might still be hit in 2036, and I cannot assume we can retire at 56.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking hall projects and ask for more supervised railing work on older buildings. We would put contract premiums toward the mortgage each year after keeping our ten-month reserve. In the first year after 2036 my partner would seek paid clinic openings if reception hours fell, while I would keep site work and ask for a real robot trial before 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years, with a serious note about the later dates. We have time to pay down what we owe and see what either employer offers. I would not ask the children to carry our uncertainty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would paying down the mortgage change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would make one wage gap easier to manage if the clinic changed first. We would check the balance every year, not use up our reserve in one grand payment. I still expect both of us to earn something at 56.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hope the children learn from this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That adults can prepare without making every dinner about fear. I would tell them work changes and we keep learning, but their school years are for learning too. They should not have to solve our loan.

say: I would say **2036 desk AI** arrives before 2039 site robots.
I would ask employers for real **robot evidence** over the decade.
think: I would be **56** at the robot date, with grown children and perhaps a smaller mortgage.
My partner’s **reception role** may change first, and retirement is not assured.
do: Keep paid **hall projects** and ask for supervised older-building rail work.
Pay contract premiums toward the **mortgage** while protecting the reserve.
Ask for a **site robot trial** before 2039 while my partner checks clinic openings.
feel: **Calm** near term, serious about both later job dates.
S4.quote: I would not ask the children to carry our uncertainty.
fieldNote: Iris uses the long warning to reduce the **mortgage**, while recognising a potential 2036 hit to reception pay.
She treats the children as **grown** by 2039 and keeps adult income decisions with herself and her partner.

steps.text: Keep paid hall projects and practice rail work on older buildings
Pay contract premiums toward the mortgage while retaining ten months of savings
Watch a real site robot trial before changing work plans

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my partner’s reception wage could be hit in 2028 and site robots follow around 2031. Clear hours from both employers, paid clinic training tied to real shifts and continued building vacancies would help. We can manage a gap, but two missing wages would change the mortgage quickly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the order in which a household loses hours. People tell a construction worker she has three extra years, but a partner at a desk may not. We need plans for both payslips, not just my tools.

headlineQuote: We need plans for both payslips, not just my tools.
portrait: Iris is a **43-year-old junior** construction worker fitting access rails, learning from a carpenter after leaving school early.
Her public contract brings **higher pay**, while a dental receptionist partner, two children and ten months saved support the mortgage.
She uses **AI occasionally** for plan terms, then checks the answer against an old wall and a skilled worker.
She watches **both wages** as thinking AI reaches reception before robots reach her hands-on rail work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens reception income first, then hands-on construction work around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **hours**, paid clinic training tied to shifts and real building vacancies would help the household plan.
